t: Our values, in practice
s: Every company has values. Most of them live on a wall in a meeting room and die
there. I want ours to live in your hands, in the decisions you make when nobody's
watching, when the day is long, when the guest is difficult, when the easy choice
and the right choice are not the same choice.
So let's go through them, not as a list to memorize, as tools to use.
Sustainability, and I always insist on saying it fully: financial, environmental,
and social sustainability. All three in that unusual order on purpose.
People are sometimes surprised I put financial first.
Let me be honest with you about why.
If Craveiral doesn't make money, everything else dies.
The farm dies, the jobs die, the mission dies.
The whole beautiful idea becomes a story about a lawyer who wasted his money on a
dream. Financial sustainability is what buys us the right to pursue everything
else. So when you avoid waste, when you take care of equipment, when you fill the
washing machine properly, when you upsell a wine you believe in, you're not being
petty, you're protecting the mission.
Environmental sustainability, you already know.
The 4% footprint, the water recycling, the composting, the regenerative farming.
And social aspect, fair work, local hiring, serving the village, being a good
neighbor. Three legs. The stool stands on all of them or it doesn't stand.
Simplicity. This one is deceptive because simplicity is hard work.
Anyone can make something complicated.
Look at our houses, minimalist design, natural materials, nothing shouting for
attention. That's a thousand decisions about what to leave out.
In your work, simplicity means don't overcomplicate the guest experience.
Clear answers, honest food, processes that make sense.
If you find yourself doing something convoluted and you don't know why, question
it. Ask. Maybe there's a reason. Maybe it's just accumulated clutter and you found
something we should simplify. Comfort and modernity.
We are rustic in soul, but we are not a museum of rural hardship.
Our guests sleep on excellent mattresses. The indoor pool is heated.
The Wi-Fi works. There are Smeg appliances and We-Wood furniture in some of the
houses. And every house has a proper kitchen and a private terrace.
Why does this matter? Because we're not asking guests to sacrifice comfort in
exchange for authenticity. The whole point of Craveiral is that they get both.
Simplicity is not scarcity. Remember that when you set up a room or serve a table,
warm, generous, comfortable, and simple.
Freedom and authenticity. Guests at Craveiral are free.
Free to do everything, surf lessons, horseback riding, hikes on the fisherman's
trail, yoga, or absolutely gloriously nothing.
Never make a guest feel they're missing out if they just want to lie by the pool
for three days. And authenticity means we don't perform.
The farm is a real farm. The eggs are real eggs from this morning.
The people are real people. You are not required to wear a corporate smile that
isn't yours. I would much rather a guest meet the real you with your real warmth
and your real accent than some hospitality school character.
Guests can smell theater from a kilometer away. What they can't resist is truth.
Creativity and community integration. Creativity.
You're allowed to have ideas. More than allowed, expected.
Some of the best things at Craveiral came from the team, not from me.
And community integration. We are of São Teotónio, not just in it.
The laundry serves the village. The shop sells our neighbors honey and wine and
olive oil. We hire locally whenever we can.
When a guest asks what to visit, we send them to the village, to Odeceixe, to
Zambujeira, to the local restaurants.
We are ambassadors for the whole territory, not gatekeepers trying to trap guests
on the property. Well-being, and this one is for the guests and for you.
A burned-out team cannot deliver warm hospitality.
It's simply not possible to give what you don't have.
So take your breaks, eat properly. Tell your manager when the load is too much.
Use the beauty of this place. You work somewhere people pay hundreds of euros a
night to be. Walk the property sometimes. Look at the coastline on your day off.
If working here doesn't include some joy, we're doing it wrong, and I want to know.
Now, values are easy when everything's fine. The test is when they conflict.
A guest wants something wasteful. Comfort versus sustainability.
A creative idea costs money. Creativity versus financial discipline.
I'm not going to pretend there's a formula. There isn't.
What I'll tell you is this: when values collide, think about the long game.
We're not trying to win a day. We're trying to build something that lasts decades.
The decision that serves the relationship with the guest, with the land, with the
team. Over the years, that's almost always the right one.
And when you're not sure, ask. Asking is never a weakness here.
Next model, we get the craft itself. Hospitality, the Craveiral way.

t: Hospitality, the Craveiral way
s: Let's talk about hospitality. The real thing, not the industry, the craft.
I want to start with a distinction that changed the way I think about this work.
There is a difference between service and hospitality. Service is technical.
The food arrives hot. The room is clean. The check-in takes five minutes.
Service is measurable, and it's mandatory. We must be excellent at it.
But hospitality is something else. Hospitality is how the guest feels.
Service happens to the guest. Hospitality happens inside the guest.
You can have perfect service and zero hospitality.
We've all been to those hotels, flawless, polished, cold as a hospital corridor.
And you can have humble service with overwhelming hospitality.
Think of your grandmother's house.
The tablecloths might not be pressed, but nobody in history has ever felt unwelcome
at their grandmother's table. Craveral has to be both, the standards of a
great hotel and the feeling of a home.
Our welcome should say what our brand says, Fica. Pertence.
Stay, belong. So how do we do that, concretely?
First, guests are guests, not customers. The word matters.
A customer is someone in a transaction. A guest is someone in your home.
When friends come to your house, you don't process them.
You open the door, you're happy to see them, you offer them something to drink.
You make them feel that their arrival improved your day. That's the posture.
Every arrival, every day, including the day you're tired, including the arrival at
22 hours when you wanted to go home.
That family drove two and a half hours from Lisbon Airport, probably with children
asleep in the back seat. Their holiday starts with your face.
Second, use names. From the reservation, from the check-in, learn
them. "Welcome back, Mrs. Keller.
How was the beach?" Costs nothing and is worth everything.
People spend their whole lives wanting to be recognized.
In a world of apps and QR codes and self-service kiosks, a person who remembers
your name is becoming a luxury. We will always offer that luxury.
Third, anticipate. The deepest hospitality answers needs the guest hasn't voiced
yet. It's cold tonight. Are the fire pits lit before someone asks?
A couple booked the owner's house for an anniversary.
Is there something waiting for them that says we noticed?
A child at dinner is melting down. Can we bring the pizza a little faster without
being asked? Watch, notice, act.
Anticipation is just attention plus initiative, and both are free.
Fourth, know the land, tell the land.
Every one of you should be able to tell a guest where to watch the sunset.
Which beach suits small children?
Carvalhal, by the way, easiest access, and our beach bar is right there.
Where the fisherman's trail is most beautiful, what medronho is, and why they
should try it. You are not staff who happen to be in Alentejo.
You are the guest's connection to this territory.
That's the belong gesture, remember. Bring those who eat closer to those who grow.
Every conversation is a chance to make that connection.
Fifth, the small rituals matter more than the grand gestures.
Guests forget the marble lobby of some five-star palace within a week.
What they remember for years, the waiter who remembered which wine they liked on
the second night, the housekeeper who arranged the child's stuffed animals on the
pillow, the receptionist who printed the boarding passes without being asked twice.
Hospitality is compound interest.
Tiny deposits made consistently that add up to a feeling of being cared for.
Let me tell you what I consider the perfect Craveral moment.
A guest once told me at checkout, and I've never forgotten it, she said,
"Pedro, the strangest thing happened to me here.
On the third day, I stopped taking photographs."
I asked her what she meant, and she said, "I realized I wasn't trying to prove I
was here. I was just here." That's it. That's the whole job.
Everything we do, the silence we protect at night, the walkways through the trees,
the food from 80 meters away, the fact that nobody is pushing an activity schedule
at anyone, all of it is engineered to help a human being arrive.
Not just check in, arrive in the deepest sense of the word.
Our guests live in cities under pressure on screens.
We give them back the rhythm of the land, sunrise, work, food, rest, stars.
When it works, it's not a holiday, it's a repair.
And you, whatever your role, you're a guardian of that repair.
The housekeeper who works quietly while a guest sleeps late is protecting it.
The gardener who waves good morning is part of it.
The waiter who doesn't rush the table under the stars is honoring it.
One last thing for this model. Warmth is not servility. We are warm.
We are generous. We are attentive. And we carry ourselves with dignity always.
You are professionals in one of the most meaningful crafts there is, taking care of
human beings. Walk like it. Never grovel, never be cold.
Between those two extremes lives everything I mean by the word hospitality.
Next model, the guest journey. From the first click to the last look in the
rearview mirror.

t: One single house
s: Nine hectares. 38 independent houses.
And only 4% of the land built on. Everything else is a working farm.
Vegetable garden, orchard, animals, pinewood, stitched together by wooden
boardwalks. If you arrived a week ago or three years ago, you probably know this.
What this module asks of you is different.
Stop seeing five units and start seeing one single house, because that is how the
guest sees it. Craveral belongs to the Belong family of brands, and Belong's
signature is giving shape to meaning.
Behind it sits a simple and demanding idea: a place that is well cared for
cares for the people in it. That is why we exist.
Not to run a hotel with a pretty garden next door.
We exist to regenerate this territory through circular economy, and we use
hospitality because it is the strongest economic and cultural engine we have
to prove it. Circular economy here is not a slogan.
It is a chain you can walk in five minutes.
The garden gives more than 70% of what the kitchen serves.
What the kitchen does not use goes to compost. The compost goes back to the garden.
What we cannot grow, we buy in the shortest radius possible: cheeses from the
region, fish from this coast, wines from the Alentejo and the Vicentina, and the
São Teotónio Laundry washes our linen and the village's.
Our back of house is itself a service to our neighbors.
We run five units: the accommodation, the farm table, Bar da Praia do Carvalhal,
the beach bar, the shop, and the São Teotónio Laundry.
Five teams, five routines, five heads.
But guests are not buying five things. They're buying Craveral.
And when the shop holds one standard and the restaurant another, they do not think
the shop is worse. They think Craveral is inconsistent.
Consistency across units is not a management detail. It is the promise.
And the house is bigger than the farm.
There is the beach bar, minutes from here, on the sand of the Costa Vicentina.
There is a Mesa do Campo. In Lisbon, at the modern art center of the Calouste
Gulbenkian Foundation, the cooking of this territory is served at a city table
inside a museum. There are the weddings, the retreats, the companies that
come here to think. Different stages, the same play.
And when you recommend something of ours, you are not selling.
You are taking the guest to more of what they already chose.
There is a part of this we say too little, and it is worth saying.
Regeneration here has to work as a business, or it is not regeneration.
It is charity in disguise. We have commitments to the house owners, to our
suppliers, to the team, and to this land.
Meeting them is not the opposite of purpose. It is the condition for it.
That is why waste bothers us so much.
Food, water, energy, time, talent, or goodwill, we waste
nothing. Because everything wasted is regeneration we can no longer pay for.
If all this works, the guest feels six things: welcomed, recognized as a
person, not processed as a booking; slowed down, with permission to do less;
cared for, without ceremony; connected to the land, the food, the people,
the village, and whoever came with them; restored, they leave lighter than they
arrived; and trusted, free to decide how they use their time here.
Those six words are your job description, whatever your role.
You leave with one question for whenever you are unsure whether something is
Craveral or not.
It is this: does this bring the person who eats closer to the person who grows?
If it does, it is ours. If it does not, it is not, however
profitable it looks. That holds for an investment decision, and it holds for how
you answer a guest on the boardwalk.
In the next modules, we go to each unit, one by one, and to the standard each one
has to hold. Stay. Belong.

t: The houses
s: If you are going to represent Craveiral, you have to know Craveiral the way you
know your own home.
This module is a visit, and it has two parts: the facts and the standard.
The facts, because confidence sells and vagueness kills.
The standard, because a house made ready is not a clean room, it is a promise kept.
We start with the facts. Thirty-eight independent houses organized in clusters,
three main clusters, plus the studios closer to the central services.
They share the same DNA, sustainability, local craft, a nod to Portuguese heritage.
Minimal but warm. Every unit has a properly equipped kitchen, organic amenities,
air conditioning, and a private terrace with table and armchairs.
And pets are welcome, which matters to more guests every year, and which we do
properly, not grudgingly. The typologies, and these you should know by heart.
Studios, 40 square meters, two guests.
Farm houses, 64 meters, one bedroom, up to four.
Farm lofts, also 64 meters, two guests.
We wood interiors in cherry and oak in the Cravo cluster, which has a private pool
for its guests. Two-bedroom houses, 85 meters foreign comfort, up to
six. Wood burner in the living room.
Farmer's house, two bedrooms, dam furniture, Smeg kitchen, two decks.
And the owner's house we wood. Our signature, 85 meters, Essence
mattress, Corca tub, a small library.
Why do we make you learn square meters? Because of this situation.
A guest asks, "Does the two-bedroom house work for us with the children?" Two
answers are possible. The vague one, "Yes, I think so,"
leaves the guest where they were. The precise one, "Yes, and if they are small, the
sofa bed in the living room gives you room to spare.
The second bedroom can be twins or a double.
Tell me which you prefer."
That answer has just built trust, and trust is the currency of this business.
The shared spaces, half of what the guest is buying.
Three pools, the big outdoor one, 24 by 9 meters for real swimming, the
heated indoor 12 by 5 with the glass-fronted sauna beside it, and the children's
pool. The wellness deck raising the pinewood.
Outdoor sauna, hot tub, cold plunge, a full thermal circuit.
The gym. The nature interpretation center, wood and glass among the pines.
Yoga twice a week, retreats, workshops, meetings, 50 seated for a banquet,
80 standing. The terrace with the fire pits and the playground area for events up
to 300 people. Now, the standard, and here the tone changes.
A standard is a promise we made to every future guest based on what we delivered to
the past ones. The guest paid for the Craveiral of the photographs and the
reviews.
Every detail right keeps that promise.
The flawless bed, the kitchen without a mark, the inviting terrace, the amenities
complete. Every detail wrong breaks it a little.
Broken promises pile up in silence. Guests rarely complain about small things.
They think less of us quietly, book elsewhere one day, and we never know why.
Hence, the rule I want you to keep. Details are not small.
Here, details are everything, because our whole promise is care.
A farm that preaches love of the land and has a dirty pool filter or a dead bulb on
a boardwalk is a contradiction the guest feels at once, even if they cannot explain
it. Coherence between what we say and what we do is our highest standard.
And one thing only guest well-being asks for gets forgotten: sleep.
Total blackout, maintenance noise at an agreed hour.
Never knocking before 10:00 in the morning unless asked.
Last point, and a test of character.
When you see something wrong that is not your job, a fallen branch on the
boardwalk, a dirty window, litter by the pool, there are two kinds of people.
The one who thinks someone should sort that out, and the one who sorts it or
reports it within the hour. Craveiral was built by the second kind.
Be the second kind. Next module, The Farm Table, where all this
philosophy lands.

t: FarmTable
s: If Craveiral has a soul, you can taste it,
literally.
This module is about the farm table, and the philosophy fits in one
line.
Before the plate, there is someone who grows.
Everything else follows. More than 70%
of what we serve is born here.
The vegetables ripened in this soil.
The herbs were cut this morning. The eggs were laid today
by hens. The guest can go and see.
What we do not grow, we buy as close as possible.
Cheeses from the region, fish from this coast,
wines from the Alentejo and the Vicentina vineyards just up the
road. Medronho from the local distillery.
The menu turns with the seasons because the farm does.
Not a limitation, the whole point.
A tomato in August here tastes like something other than a supermarket tomato
in January.
That is what root to table means.
Not marketing decoration, but a supply chain
you can walk in five minutes.
Breakfast is a statement of identity, and I treat it as one.
House breads, our jams, local cheeses, farm eggs
cooked to order.
Generous, honest, unhurried. Many guests will tell
you at checkout that breakfast was the best part of the day.
That is normal and a compliment worth protecting.
At lunch and dinner,
seasonal, simple, satisfying.
Dishes with character, made with care.
Inside in the light-filled room or out on the terrace with the garden and the
Alentejo evening. And the pizzas, because guests will talk about them.
The outdoor wood oven is one of the most loved things on this property.
Sun-ripened tomato, herbs picked here, local
cheeses, fire.
Children make their own in the pizza classes and eat their creation with a
pride worth photographing.
Never talk the pizza down for being humble.
The wood oven on a summer night, children on the grass, the fire pits
being lit.
That is Craveiral at full power.
Wine.
You do not need to be a sommelier.
You need three sentences. Where it is from, what it is like,
what it goes with. Example,
this white comes from vineyards near the coast.
20 minutes from here. Fresh, slightly saline, exactly
what the fish is asking for.
Done.
That sells the wine, honors the producer, and connects the guest to the
territory. Three sentences. And the preserves,
jams, and ferments.
The old crafts.
Explaining that a jam exists because July gave more fruit than we
could serve fresh teaches regeneration with a spoon.
Now service, where this module is decided.
Four principles, and they are hard.
One, never rush a table.
We are the antidote to the city, and the long meal is the ceremony of
this place.
The table under the stars, the second bottle, the conversation that stretches,
protect that.
Efficiency belongs to the kitchen.
At the table, what counts is presence.
Two, tell the chain.
Every dish has a story, and the story is true.
Not a lecture, one line.
The courgettes are from the garden, picked this morning.
One line changes the meal.
Three,
honesty about what we are.
We are not a temple of tweezers and foams, but honest cooking,
excellent and with soul, from a working farm.
Own that with pride.
Anyone wanting a starred performance has other addresses.
Anyone wanting to taste a territory has us, and there are
far more of them. Four, dietary requirements are
hospitality, not a nuisance.
Allergies, intolerances, vegetarians, the child who only
eats pasta. Each is a person hoping not to be a
problem.
A kitchen that improvises a beautiful vegetarian dish without
sighing wins a family for good.
The farm table is not only this room.
It is the same kitchen that goes to the weddings, the companies, and the
Mesa do Com in a museum in Lisbon.
One kitchen philosophy, many tables.
The gesture is always the same.
Bring the person who eats closer to the person who grows.
A closing thought. Food is where trust becomes physical.
The guest hands us their hunger three times a day, and there is
something old and intimate in that.
Feed people as if it mattered, because here it
does.

t: Bar da Praia do Carvalhal
s: On the sand of the Costa Vicentina, minutes from Craveiral,
is the beach our guests use most.
The easiest access on this stretch of coast, the one families
prefer.
That is where Bar da Praia do Carvalhal is,
and the shortest definition I can give you is this:
the beach bar is the Craveiral philosophy in flip-flops.
Easier, looser, more informal,
never more careless.
There is a temptation in this unit, and it is worth naming.
Because the register is more informal, it is easy to let the standard
slide with it.
They are not the same thing.
Informal means no linen tablecloth and no formal
address.
It does not mean a badly washed glass, a toilet nobody is
checking, or a 20-minute wait with nobody saying anything.
The register changes, the standard does not.
If you keep one line from this module, keep that one.
And there is something the bar team needs to see clearly.
To anyone walking off that beach and into the bar, you are
Craveiral.
Many of those people have never slept on the farm and perhaps never will.
That glass, that plate, that good morning, is the only sample
of the brand they will get.
A good hour in that bar sells room nights we will
never be able to attribute to anyone.
A bad hour closes doors we never knew we closed.
The menu follows the same logic as the house: honest, simple,
with an origin.
Fish from this coast, products from the region, wines we
know the source of, and whatever the farm can send.
The chain is told here as it is told at the farm table.
Only instead of a sentence at the table,
it is a sentence at the counter in five seconds.
"This is from our garden, 20 minutes
from here."
Five seconds.
Nobody is in a hurry for a lecture on the beach, but everyone warms
to something true.
The bar is also where the surf lessons start, booked through
reception.
And here is the rhythm of the perfect day, which I want you to know by
heart because it is the best recommendation we have.
Morning on the farm, lunch and afternoon at Carvalhal,
dinner under the stars back home.
Recommending the beach is not sending the guest out of the business,
it is moving them inside it.
And when reception says this on arrival,
the guest feels somebody thought about their day.
That is hospitality, not selling.
Two operational demands the beach makes and the farm does not.
The first is time.
On the beach, people get hungry at unpredictable hours and
have short patience under the sun.
A wait time communicated,
"It is 20 minutes. Shall I bring you water meanwhile?"
settles 90% of complaints before they exist.
What generates a complaint is not waiting.
It is waiting without information.
The second is sun and water.
Shade, cold water, toilets checked hourly,
attention to children and older people at midday.
Wellbeing on the beach is mostly reducing physical discomfort
nobody puts into words.
And because we are on a Costa Vicentina beach inside a protected
area,
there is a coherence that is not negotiable.
We do not let plastic loose in the wind.
We collect what is ours and some of what is not.
We close the day with the sand in front of us better than we found
it.
A bar that lives off the beauty of that coast and dirties it, is the
most visible contradiction this group can produce.
And it is visible to hundreds of people a day, not to an
annual audit. Your module in three things.
You change the register,
never the standard.
To anyone coming out of that water, you are the whole of Craveiral.
And what you serve has an origin you can tell in five seconds.
The rest is what you already know how to do.
Be present,
see before you are asked,
and treat that counter as if it were your own living room,
because it is.
In the next module, the shop, the territory condensed and
portable.

t: The Shop
s: The shop is the most misunderstood thing at Craviol.
Seen as a place that sells souvenirs, it is a small shop with a tight margin.
Seen as what it actually is, the territory condensed and portable.
It becomes one of the most effective brand tools we have.
This module is about the second reading.
What we carry: local wines, craft rum, small production honey, jams,
olive oil, infusions, soaps and body oils made nearby by traditional methods,
and comfortable clothing inspired by farm life. At first glance, a selection.
In fact, it is a map. Every shelf is a producer, and almost all of them are less
than half an hour's drive from here.
The shop is the only place on the property where the guest can literally put the
territory in their suitcase. And here is the only sales technique I will ask of
you. One sentence about origin turns a souvenir into a relationship.
Compare, "This honey is very good," what any shop says, with,
"This honey comes from a producer 20 minutes from here.
His hives are in the eucalyptus woods, and the taste changes from year to year with
the flowering." The second costs no more time, is not pushy, and turns a jar of
honey into an object with a story the guest will tell at home.
Minimum target, five products, five stories by heart.
There is something about when the shop happens that changes everything.
The memory of a stay is not an average.
It forms mostly at the most intense moment and at the last one.
And the shop is often the last place the guest is before getting into the car.
So the shop is not a commercial extra at the end.
It is one of the two pieces that weigh most in the memory they take away.
A cold shop with little attention wipes out three good days.
A warm one closes the stay on a high note. Two things we do not do.
We do not push. The practical rule, we recommend what we would recommend to a
friend, and we stop the first time the guest hesitates.
A, "No, thank you," taken naturally preserves the relationship.
A second argument after the no ruins it. And we do not inflate.
If a product is not organic, we do not say it is.
If that olive oil is not our production, we say whose it is.
With pride, because it belongs to someone from this land.
Honesty about origin is what gives origin its value.
The physical standard of the shop has its own rules, and they are harder than they
look, because a small shop does not forgive disorder.
Shelves full, but not piled. Labels legible and all facing front.
Nothing dusty.
And in a farm setting with doors open, that means checking daily, not weekly.
Nothing out of date ever. And no stock outs on the 10 best-selling products.
If the honey runs out in August, the problem is not August, it is the July order.
And the shop is a listening tool we are not using well.
Whoever is in the shop hears things that reach nobody else.
What the guest says they wish they could find and cannot.
What they praise without knowing it is praise. What they say about price.
It is the only conversation of the stay where the guest is comparing us with the
real world. Write it down. One line per shift at the end of the day,
somewhere shared. Three months of that is worth more than a market study.
I will close with the underlying reason.
Every product that leaves that shop is money that stays in this region with a
producer who lives half an hour away.
A bottle of wine sold there is circular economy happening on a small scale.
And small is where this gets done. When you explain an origin to a guest,
you are not selling a jar. You are doing the work the whole brand says it came here
to do. In the next module, the São Teotónio laundry, where circular economy
is seen closer still.

t: The São Teotónio laundry
s: This is the module a lot of people will assume has nothing to do with them.
It does. The São Teotónio Laundry is the least visible unit at Craveiral,
and probably the easiest way to explain circular economy to anyone who doubts
it. Because here, there is no metaphor.
A laundry set up to serve a hotel operation also serves the village it sits in.
That is it.
Circular economy in the plainest clothes there are.
It is worth seeing what the alternative would have been.
A 38-house hotel on the Costa Vicentina normally hands its linen to an industrial
operator in a city an hour or more away.
Lorries covering that distance every week. Jobs created in another municipality.
Nothing for São Teotónio. Building this here traded all of that for local
employment, money circulating in this parish, and a service the village did not
have and now does. Now the part that matters to anyone in accommodation.
Linen is the most intimate physical contact the guest has with Craveiral.
Eight hours a night with their skin against our sheet.
They touch our towels straight out of the shower when they are most sensitive to
everything. No amenity, no view, no dish makes up for a
rough sheet or a towel that smells damp.
This unit's work goes straight into the guest's sleep, and sleep is the most
decisive well-being indicator of a stay.
The standard is measured in four things.
Correct sorting on the way in, by type, by soiling, by temperature.
Most damage happens before the machine starts. Stain protocol on the first pass.
A stain that goes through the dryer once never comes out. Traceability.
We know which linen is from which house and which day, and what is out of
circulation and why. And the rejection without hesitation.
A piece with a hole, a set stain, or fraying never goes back on a bed.
Cheaper to lose the piece than the guest. Water and energy.
A laundry is by nature the unit that consumes the most water and the most energy
per square meter in the whole group.
Which means it is also where a good decision is worth most.
A full load instead of a half load. The right temperature, not the highest out of
habit. Measured dosing, not by eye.
Machine maintenance on a schedule, not on a breakdown.
None of this is decorative ecology.
It is the same waste nothing logic we apply in the kitchen applied where the
numbers are bigger. And the service to the village which asks something not
obvious. The neighbor who brings in a bag of washing is not a lesser customer
because they do not sleep in one of our houses.
Same treatment, same turnaround, same courtesy. On principle.
We said we would open our doors to the village, and integration is judged by that,
not by press releases. In practice, those people are our neighbors.
Some will be our colleagues, and all of them talk about us in the café.
Local reputation is built one exchange at a time.
A word to the heads, because this unit carries a specific risk.
It is physically demanding work in heat with little visibility and little
spontaneous recognition. No guest writes a review praising the laundry, and our
internal principle is explicit. We treat the team as we expect the team to treat
the guest, and the standard is the same.
In practice, breaks taken in August and not only in November, thermal conditions
checked, and recognition said out loud when the work is good, because here, nobody
else will say it. To close, a farm that preaches love of the land
and runs a laundry wasting water is the same contradiction as a dead bulb on a
boardwalk. Except nobody sees it, which makes it easier to let happen.
Coherence is the highest standard we have, and it is measured where nobody is
looking. The short version. The back of house is the proof that the promise is
true. In the last two modules, we leave the units for what runs through all of
them, experience and well-being.

t: Experiential tourism
s: There is a difference between an activity and an experience, and it is not
vocabulary. An activity is something the guests did.
An experience is something they take away.
The same harvest at 5:00 in the afternoon with the same people can be either.
And what decides? It is not the script or the equipment. It is how it is led.
This model gives you the tool to decide that on purpose, not by luck.
The tool has four registers from research into the experience economy.
Any moment you offer lives in four dimensions.
Aesthetic, the guest is somewhere beautiful and needs to do nothing.
Educational, they learn something new.
Escapist, they take part, they choose, they get their hands dirty.
Entertainment, they enjoy themselves, they laugh.
Memorable experiences touch all four. Weak ones stay in one.
And most badly designed activities get stuck in the educational, someone explaining
things to people standing still. Apply it to the harvest, our most common
experience. Aesthetic, arriving at the garden late in the afternoon and just being
there because the light does the work. Do not fill it with information.
Educational, one thing, one only, that they did not know.
Why this courgette exists in August and not January.
Escapist, they cut, they pick, they choose.
If they only watch, it is a demonstration.
Entertainment, something that makes them laugh.
The hen that follows them, the child who finds an egg.
Second rule, choice instead of a program.
The value a guest puts on an experience rises when they help decide what to do, not
only do it. In practice, a different sentence.
Instead of, "Tomorrow at 10:00, there is a harvest," we say,
"Tomorrow there is a harvest at 10:00, and bread at 5:00. Both one.
Or would you rather keep the morning free?" The option of doing nothing has to be
on the table set by us. That makes the rest an invitation, not a timetable.
Third rule, the first 90 seconds. Arrival sets the expectation for the whole stay.
The only moment with no second chance. The standard.
Recognized by name, take the bag, offer water, drop the pace immediately.
We do not check in at the counter if we can avoid it. We walk and talk.
One or two real questions. "First time with us?
Anything we should know to make this better?" And we listen to the answer.
Ninety seconds done well. By margin for three days.
Fourth rule, the peak and the end. Memory forms at the peak and at the end,
not on the average. Two consequences. One, guarantee a deliberate peak per stay.
Dinner under the stars, the sauna at dusk, bread out of the oven.
A stay can be entirely correct and have no peak, and no peak means no
recommendation. Two, the goodbye can never be the weakest
moment. A rushed departure wipes out three good days.
A genuine farewell, help with the luggage, a small gesture from the farm, an
invitation to return that does not sound commercial.
Fifth rule, whoever leads has to know the land, not the script.
An experience led by someone who memorized a text is obvious within 30 seconds.
Led by someone who knows what goes on here, it takes any question and survives the
rain, the delay, the difficult group.
And when a guest asks something you cannot answer, which will happen, do not
invent. Take them to someone who knows, then learn the answer for next time.
That is not failure. Inventing is.
And the last, cross-recommendation is hospitality, not selling.
Sending a guest from the pool to the beach bar, or a couple who love dinner into a
conversation about weddings, takes them to more of what they already chose.
The practical distinction, recommend what you would recommend to a friend, and stop
at the first hesitation. Five rules then.
The four registers, choice instead of a program, 90 seconds, peak and
end, and whoever leads knows the land.
Last module, wellbeing, guest, and team.
And what to do when something goes wrong.

t: Wellbeing and service recovery
s: This module has two halves that look separate and are not.
The first is about wellbeing. Our stay here leaves a person better than it found
them. The second is what to do when something goes wrong.
The moment any hospitality career is truly tested. The link is simple.
Most of the wellbeing we offer does not come from what we add.
It comes from what we avoid and what we fix fast.
First lever, dose of nature. A study of nearly 20,000 people
found the association between contact with nature and reported wellbeing plateaus
at around two hours a week. You will not quote that to a guest, but see
what it means. Our competitive advantage is dose of nature, and nine
hectares with 4% build are only worth it if the guest leaves the house.
Your job is to reduce friction, the map in their hand, the harvest basket at the
door, the blanket on the deck. Second lever, sleep.
It is the strongest wellbeing determinant of a stay.
Almost always compromised by operational causes, not design.
Total blackout verified, not assumed. Maintenance noise at an agreed hour.
Nighttime quiet explained warmly on arrival, not as a house rule, and never
knocking on a door before 10:00 in the morning without an express request.
People who sleep well forgive almost anything.
People who sleep badly forgive nothing.
And the reason given in the review is rarely sleep. Third lever, choice.
Control over your own time is one of the strongest recovery factors there is, which
is why freedom is a value of ours, not a brochure adjective.
We do not over-program, over-explain, or interrupt.
Fourth, quiet and pace.
We are the antidote to the city with concrete consequences.
No rushing a table, no loud music at the pool at 3:00 in the afternoon, no
vacuuming a corridor at 8:30. In doubt between adding and removing, remove.
Before complaints, the list of what must never happen because it is the source of
most of them. A guest in front of a team member who does not acknowledge them.
A guest passed between three people for a simple question.
A guest waiting without knowing why.
A guest hearing two versions of the same answer.
A guest sensing the team in conflict or short-staffed.
A guest forced to repeat themselves.
And worst, a guest who leaves with a complaint we never knew about.
The protocol, four steps in this order.
One, acknowledge immediately and without defending.
You do not argue with a guest's perception, you deal with it. Two, own it.
Whoever hears a complaint owns it until it is resolved, even if the fix belongs to
another department. Passing it on is not resolving it.
Following through is. Three, resolve within the hour.
If that is impossible, report back every hour until it is done.
Silence turns a problem into an incident.
Four, close the loop. One contact before departure confirming it was resolved.
The most forgotten step and the one weighing most on the final rating. Two notes.
First, a problem solved within the hour is a story the guest tells friends.
A problem that drags on is a story they tell on a review platform.
Speed is not courtesy, it is strategy.
Second, you do not buy a guest's forgiveness.
Research in hospitality shows a well-recovered failure can generate as much loyalty
as faultless service or more. But also that overcompensation backfires,
shifting the gesture from care to transaction.
Resolve, acknowledge, offer a proportionate gesture.
Not three free nights for a tap.
And the half that closes this series.
We treat the team as we expect the team to treat the guest, and the standard is the
same. Not a nice statement. Three behaviors from the heads.
Breaks taken in August and not only in November.
A reported error handled at no personal cost to whoever reported it.
The problem is not the error, it is hiding it.
And shift handover as a transfer of care, not an end of responsibility.
Standards drift when people are tired. Stay. Belong.

t: FarmTable: where the philosophy becomes food
s: If Craveiral has a soul, you can taste it,
literally.
This module is about the farm table and about food, which
if you know me at all, you know is the part of this project I could
talk about for six hours instead of 10 minutes.
I'll restrain myself.
Let me start with the philosophy, and it fits in one sentence.
Before the plate, there is a grower.
Everything else follows from that.
Over 70% of what we serve is grown on this
property. The vegetables ripened in our soil.
The herbs were cut this morning. The eggs were laid today by
hens you can walk over and meet. What we don't grow, we
source as close as possible.
Cheeses from the region, fish from this coast, wines from
Alentejo, and from the Vicentino vineyards up the road, Medronho from
the local distillery. The menu rotates with the seasons because the
farm rotates with the seasons.
And that's not a limitation, it's the entire point.
A tomato in August here tastes like a different food from a supermarket tomato
in January.
Our guests come, in part, to remember what food
actually tastes like. This is what root to table means when we
say it. Not a marketing garnish, a supply chain you
can walk in five minutes.
Breakfast. I said it before and I'll say it again.
Breakfast is a statement of identity.
House-made breads, our own preserves, local cheeses,
farm eggs cooked to order,
generous, honest, unhurried.
Many guests will tell you at checkout that breakfast was their favorite part of the
day. That's normal, and it's a compliment to protect.
Lunch and dinner, seasonal, simple, satisfying.
Dishes with character, prepared with care and creativity.
Indoors in the light-filled dining room, or outside on the terrace with
the garden and the Alentejo evening.
And the pizzas.
Let's talk about the pizzas, because guests certainly will.
The outdoor wood-fired oven is one of the most beloved things on this
property. Sun-ripened tomatoes, just-picked
herbs, local cheeses, fire.
Children make their own in the pizza classes and eat their creation with a
pride you can photograph.
Never look down on the pizza because it's humble.
The wood-fired pizza on a summer evening, kids
running on the grass, fire pits starting to glow.
That image is Craveiral working at full power.
Wine. You know my weakness. Our list celebrates
Alentejo,
the bold reds, the balanced whites, the artisanal blends.
And I want every front of house person to be able to guide a guest through
it without fear.
You don't need to be a sommelier. You need three sentences per wine.
Where it's from, what it's like, what it loves to be
eaten with.
This white comes from vineyards near the coast, 20 minutes from
here.
It's fresh, a little saline, and it's exactly what
the fish wants.
That's it. That sentence sells the wine, honors the
winemaker, and deepens the guest's connection to the territory.
Three sentences.
And fermentation, preservation,
the old arts. Our preserves, our jams, the pickles,
the way we extend the garden's abundance across the seasons.
This is ancestral intelligence.
The circular economy existed in every Alentejo pantry
long before anyone gave it a name.
When you explain to a guest that this jam exists because the orchard gave us
more fruit in July than we could serve fresh,
you're teaching regeneration with a spoon.
Now, service at the farm table.
A few principles I hold are:
never rush a table.
We are the antidote to the city, and the long meal is the
ceremony of this place.
The table under the stars, the second bottle, the conversation that
stretches,
protect it. Efficiency matters in the kitchen.
At the table, presence matters more.
Tell the chain.
Every dish has a story, and the story is true. Use it.
Not a lecture, one line.
The courgettes are from the garden, picked this morning.
One line changes the meal.
Honesty about what we are.
We're not a gastronomic temple with tweezers and foam.
We are honest, excellent, soulful cooking from a working farm.
Own that identity with pride.
The guest who wants a Michelin performance has other addresses.
The guest who wants to taste a territory has us.
And there are many, many more of the second kind.
Dietary needs are hospitality, not hassle.
Allergies, intolerances, vegetarians, children who eat
nothing but pasta.
Every one of these is a person hoping not to be a problem.
Make them feel like they're not.
The kitchen that improvises a beautiful vegetarian plate without
sighing has just won a family's loyalty
forever.
And remember, the farm table is also the village's table, in a
sense. The restaurant, the events, the catering that
takes our kitchen to weddings and companies.
A mesa do campo taking this territory's cuisine to a museum in
Lisbon. One kitchen philosophy, many tables.
The gesture, always the same. Bring those who eat closer
to those who grow.
Last thought for this module.
Food is where trust becomes physical.
A guest entrusts their hunger three times a day.
There's something ancient and intimate about that.
Feed people like you mean it.
Because here, we do.
Next module, the constellation beyond the farm, the beach bar,
Lisbon, events,
and how it all holds together.

t: The constellation: Beach Bar, A Mesa do CAM, events, and one same gesture
s: So far, we've mostly stood on the farm.
In this module, I want to lift your eyes to the whole constellation, because Belong
is bigger than the property line, and whichever unit you work in, you're part of
all of it. Bar da Praia do Carvalhal.
On the sand of the Costa Vicentina, minutes from Craveiral, at the beach our guests
use most. Easiest access on this stretch of coast, the family favorite.
The beach bar is Craveiral's philosophy in flip-flops.
Honest food and drinks, the sea, slow time, the same care.
It's also where surf lessons happen, arranged through reception.
For many guests, the rhythm of a perfect day is exactly this.
Morning on the farm, lunch and afternoon at Carvalhal, dinner under the stars
back home. When you recommend the beach, you're not sending guests away from the
business. You're moving them around inside it.
And for the beach bar team, you are Craveiral to everyone who walks off that beach.
Same standards, same warmth with sand between your toes.
A Mesa do CAM, in Lisbon, at the modern art center of the Calouste Gulbenkian
Foundation, one of the most respected cultural institutions in the country.
Think about what that pairing means.
The cuisine of this territory served at the table of the city inside a museum.
The land at the city's table. I'm deeply proud of this one because it completes the
circle in a way nothing else does. A person has lunch at the CAM,
asks where these flavors come from, and three months later, they're sleeping in a
house in São Teotónio. Or the reverse.
A guest goes home to Lisbon and finds us again beside the art.
Each place feeds the other. Catering and events.
The purpose doesn't stay on the farm. We take the table wherever it's asked for.
Long table dinners in private homes, team experiences for companies, celebrations.
Tell us the place. We bring the land.
Same root to table kitchen, same chain, same care wherever it happens.
And the events at Craveiral itself deserve their own moment because they're
becoming a bigger part of who we are. Weddings.
From intimate ceremonies under the pines to full weekend celebrations with the
interpretation center for up to 80 standing, the restaurant and terrace, the
playground area for the big ones, up to 300 or 400, and the Craveu Cluster for a
wedding where everyone stays together around the pool.
A wedding is the highest stakes hospitality there is.
Someone's most important day, one chance, no rehearsal.
When there's a wedding on the property, everyone, whatever your role, is on the
wedding team. Corporate retreats.
Companies come here to think, reconnect, and breathe.
Nature does half the work, we do the other half.
Family celebrations, wellness getaways, retreats at the interpretation center.
Every one of these is the same product underneath.
This land, this food, this care, shaped to a moment.
Now, why am I showing you the whole constellation? Two reasons.
First, practical. Cross recommendation is how the circle turns.
The guest at the pool should hear about the beach bar.
The couple who love dinner should know we do weddings.
The Lisbon diner at the CAM should learn there's a farm behind those flavors with
beds. Nobody's pushing sales. You're connecting people to more of what they
already love. That's not selling. That's hospitality with a longer memory.
Second, deeper. I want you to understand the shape of what we're building.
One idea, a place well cared for, cares for those who inhabit it, expressed at a
farm, on a beach, in a museum, at a wedding. Different stages, same play.
If you ever wonder whether some decision fits Belong, test it against the gesture.
Does this bring those who eat closer to those who grow?
Does it make the territory stronger? Does it keep the value circulating here?
If yes, it's us. If no, it isn't. However
profitable it looks. And one honest word about growth, because you'll hear
things, and I prefer you hear them from me. Yes, we have ambitions.
New projects, new partnerships, ideas at various stages.
Some will happen, some won't. What I can promise you is that growth for us is
never expansion for its own sake. Every new point in the constellation has to
regenerate something. A building, a community, a piece of land.
Or we don't do it. We grow the way the farm grows, season by
season, roots first. You join the company that is trying to prove
something to an entire industry. That hospitality can give back more than it takes.
Every unit in this constellation is an argument in that proof, and every shift
you work is a line in the argument. Next module.
The moment every hospitality career is really tested, when things go wrong.

t: The guest journey: from first click to farewell
s: Every guest who arrives at Craveiral is on a journey that started long before the
M501 brought them to our gate and finishes long after they leave.
In this module, I want to walk that whole journey with you stage by stage, because
each of you owns a piece of it and it helps enormously to see the whole.
Stage one, the dream.
Before anything, someone is at home in Lisbon, in Munich, in London, scrolling,
dreaming of escape. They see our photographs, the houses among the trees, the long
table, the coastline. At this stage, we've made a promise.
Everything our marketing shows, the aesthetics, the calm, the farm, is a promise
that the operation, meaning you, will have to keep. I take this seriously.
We never promise what we can't deliver.
Our photos are real, our words are real, which means the bar is exactly where it
should be. Reality has to match the dream. That's hard.
That's also the job. Stage two, booking and the time before.
Someone chose us over hundreds of alternatives.
From that moment, they're already our guest, months before arrival.
Every email answered quickly and warmly, every question about cots or dogs or
dietary restrictions handled with care builds their confidence that they chose
well. And remember, we favor direct bookings.
When guests book directly through craveiral.pt, more of the value stays in the
circle, and we can take better care of them.
When you talk to potential guests, that's always the best path for them and for us.
Stage three, the arrival. Two and a half hours from Lisbon, 90 minutes
from the Algarve. Guests arrive tired, sometimes lost, often with kids who've had
enough. The first 15 minutes at Craveiral set the emotional tone for the entire
stay. I'd honestly say the first 15 minutes are worth the next three days.
A genuine welcome, a cold drink, a calm, unhurried explanation of the house and the
property. Never a bureaucratic check-in.
The message underneath every word and gesture must be, "You made it.
You can let go now." Stage four, the first morning.
This is where Craveiral really begins.
The guest wakes without an alarm for the first time in months. Rosemary in the air.
Breakfast. And our breakfast is a statement of identity.
House-made breads, our preserves, local cheeses, eggs laid that morning, cooked
how they want them. The first morning is when the guest decides, mostly
unconsciously, whether this place is what it promised.
Make the first morning perfect, and the whole stay tilts toward joy.
Stage five, the days.
And here, the guiding principle is freedom. Some guests want everything.
Surf at Carvoeiro, horseback riding on the coast, the boat on the Mira River,
hiking to Zambujeira, yoga, massage, the thermal circuit on the wellness deck in
the pines. Others want the precise opposite.
Pool, book, wine, repeat. Both are perfect stays.
Our art is reading which guest is which, offering without pushing, informing
without pressuring. And for families, the kids' pizza classes, the animals, the
eggs in the morning, the bikes. A child who feeds a goat at 8:00 in the morning has
already made the family's holiday.
Children are not an inconvenience at Craveiral, they're the guests whose memories
last longest. Stage six, the friction points.
Let me be honest about where the journey typically strains, because pretending
otherwise doesn't help you. Housekeeping timing. Guests are out.
Guests are in. Coordinating is genuinely hard.
Restaurant capacity on peak nights.
The distances on the property, beautiful, but a long walk with luggage in August
heat needs help offered proactively. Weather.
An Atlantic storm in April can bruise a beach holiday, and that's exactly when we
shine or fail. The heated indoor pool, the saunas, the fireplace, the long
lunch. A rainy day at Craveiral should be remembered as the cosiest day of the
trip, not the lost one. Know these friction points.
Own them before the guest feels them. Stage seven, the farewell.
Departures matter as much as arrivals. The psychology is real.
People remember peaks and endings. Never let a departure be reduced to an invoice.
A warm goodbye, a genuine, "Come back," maybe something small from the
shop or the farm for the road. The last image in the rearview mirror should feel
like leaving a friend's house. Stage eight, after.
The journey doesn't end at the gate.
There's the review they'll write, and reviews are the modern word of mouth.
They decide whether the next dreamer in Munich clicks on us or on someone else.
There's the memory that ripens over months, and there's the return.
Our best guests come back year after year, and some have become genuine friends of
the house. That's the real measure of everything I've described.
Not whether they were satisfied, whether they'll be back.
Here's the mental exercise I want to leave you with.
Whatever your role, locate yourself on this journey.
Which stages do you touch? Housekeeping touches four and five every single day.
Reception touches nearly all of them. The kitchen owns stage four's magic.
Maintenance quietly protects every stage at once.
Nobody at Craveiral is outside the journey.
Once you see the map, you'll never again think of your work as tasks.
It's a relay, and the baton is the guest's trust.
Next module, the houses, the farm, and the standards we keep.

t: When things go wrong: complaints and service recovery
s: Let's talk about the moments nobody puts on Instagram.
The complaint at the front desk, the dish sent back, the guest who arrives already
angry, the review that stings. If you work in hospitality long enough,
and I hope you will, these moments are guaranteed.
So instead of pretending they won't happen, let's get genuinely good at them.
First, a reframe that took me years to truly believe.
A complaint is a gift. I know how that sounds, but think it through.
A guest who complains is giving us two things, information, something in our
operation is broken, and now we know.
And a second chance, because the guest who complains to us is the guest who still
wants the stay to work. The dangerous guest is the silent one, says everything is
fine, goes home, writes the review, never returns, and we never even knew.
So when someone complains to your face, however uncomfortable, the situation is
already better than the alternative.
Breathe, and receive it like the useful thing it is. Now, the method.
When a guest is upset, there's a sequence, and the order matters.
Listen completely.
Don't defend, don't explain, don't interrupt, don't reach for the solution yet.
An upset person cannot hear solutions until they feel heard. Let them finish.
Look at them. Nod. Sometimes 30 seconds of real listening
solves half the problem, because half the problem was feeling ignored.
Acknowledge the feeling honestly.
"I'm sorry
that's not the stay we wanted you to have." You're not admitting legal fault,
you're recognizing a human being's disappointment.
It costs nothing, and it changes everything.
And please, never, ever say but. "I'm sorry, but..."
erases the apology. If there's context to explain, it can come later once things
are calm. Fix it bigger than expected.
And here's a rule I'll come back to in the final module. You have autonomy.
The cold dish doesn't just come back hot, it comes back with a glass of wine.
The room that wasn't ready earns a proper gesture, not a shrug.
The recovery should be slightly larger than the failure. Why?
Because psychology is real. A problem beautifully recovered creates more loyalty
than no problem at all. Guests forget smooth stays.
They tell everyone about the place that made a mistake and then made it
magnificently right. Follow up. The next morning, someone asks, "How
was everything last night after we sorted things out?" That 30-second question
tells the guest the care was real, not a technique.
And then this part is internal and it's non-negotiable, report it.
Every complaint goes into the system, however small, however resolved.
Not to blame anyone, because a complaint that reaches me as data is how we fix the
root cause. If three guests in a month mention the same thing, that's not three
incidents. That's one broken process wearing three costumes.
The team that hides small complaints condemns itself to repeating them forever.
A word about unfair complaints because they exist. Sometimes the guest is wrong.
Sometimes the weather is our fault in their eyes, or the expectation was
impossible.
Two things. First, you can acknowledge a feeling without agreeing with the claim.
I understand this ruined your morning is true even when we did nothing wrong.
Second, you never have to accept abuse. Rudeness, we absorb professionally.
Genuine aggression toward the team, we do not.
If a guest crosses that line, step back and call your manager.
Protecting your dignity is part of my job, and I take it seriously. And reviews.
Read them, even the harsh ones, especially the harsh ones.
A review is a complaint we didn't get to hear in person, so hear it now.
We respond to everyone, always with class, never defensively.
A future guest reading our answer to an angry review learns more about us than from
10 five-star raves. One story to close.
Years ago, a family arrived to a house that wasn't ready.
A real failure, ours, end of a brutal changeover day.
The team member at reception didn't hide behind procedure.
She sat the family on the terrace, brought drinks and pizza from the oven for the
kids, walked them through the farm to meet the animals while housekeeping finished,
and by the time they reached the house, the children were begging to stay an extra
night. That family has come back. I'm not exaggerating.
Every single year since. The mistake wasn't the story, the recovery was.
That's the standard, not perfection.
We're humans running a farm, a kitchen, and 38 houses in the Alentejo countryside.
The standard is when we drop something, we pick it up beautifully.
Next module, sustainability. Not the philosophy this time, the daily practice.
What it actually asks of you before lunch.

t: The houses, the farm, and the standards we keep
s: If you're going to represent Craveral, you need to know Craveral properly, in
detail, the way you know your own home. This module is a tour.
Some of this you know. I want all of you to know all of it.
Start with the big picture. Nine hectares, 38 independent houses
arranged in clusters, three main clusters of houses, plus studios closer to the
central facilities. Only 4% of the land is built.
The rest is working farm, orchards, vegetable gardens, animals, and pine forest,
all stitched together by those raised wooden walkways. The houses.
Every one is independent, minimalist but warm, each with its own character, and all
of them share the same DNA: sustainability, local craftsmanship, homage to
Portuguese heritage. Every unit has a proper equipped kitchen, organic amenities,
air conditioning, and a private terrace with table and armchairs. Pets are welcome.
This matters to more guests every year, and we do it properly, not grudgingly.
Know your unit types. The studios, 40 square meters, sleep two.
The farmhouses, 64 square meters, one bedroom, sleep four.
The farm lofts, also 64 square meters, sleep two.
We wood the core in cherry and oak, and part of the Craveu Cluster, which has its
own private pool for its guests. The two-bedroom houses, 85
square meters, sleep four comfortably, up to six.
With the wood-burning stove in the living room, the farmer's house, two bedrooms,
damn furniture, SMEG kitchen, two outdoor decks, and the owner's house.
We wood, our signature. 85 square meters, Essent mattress, cork
bath, a small library. The house I'd show a magazine.
Why am I making you learn square meters and bed widths?
Because confidence sells, and vagueness kills.
When a guest asks, "Would the two-bedroom work for us with the kids?" The team
member who answers precisely, "Yes.
And if the kids are small, the sofa bed in the living room gives you flexibility.
The second bedroom can be twins or a double.
Tell me which." That person has just created trust.
Trust is the currency of this whole business. The shared spaces.
Three swimming pools. The big outdoor one, 24 by 9 meters, proper laps.
The heated indoor pool, 12 by 5, with the glass-front sauna beside it.
And the children's outdoor pool. The wellness deck, raised in the pine forest.
Outdoor sauna, hot tub, cold plunge. A real thermal circuit. The gym.
The nature interpretation center, wood and glass in the pines, which hosts yoga
twice a week, retreats, workshops, meetings, and seats up to 50 for a banquet, or
80 standing. The terrace with the fire pits between the restaurant and the pool,
and the playground area, which can host events up to 300 banquet style.
The farm. This is not decoration, and I need everyone to internalize that.
The farm provides most of what our kitchen serves.
Over 70% of the restaurant's ingredients are grown on-site.
Vegetable gardens, fruit orchards, herbs, free-range eggs.
Guests are invited to walk it, to harvest seasonal produce, to meet the animals, to
cook what they pick in their own kitchenette if they like. Nothing is wasted.
Everything is connected. Field to fork, earth to plate, scraps to compost,
compost to field. When a guest asks a farm question you can't answer, that's fine.
Walk them to someone who can, and then learn the answer yourself for next time.
The shop. Local wines, artisanal rums, small batch honey, jams, olive oil,
herbal teas, natural soaps, and body oils made nearby with traditional methods.
Comfortable clothing inspired by farm life.
The shop is the territory, condensed and portable.
Every product has a story and a producer. Learn a few of them.
This honey comes from a producer 20 minutes from here, turns a souvenir into a
relationship. And the laundry in São Teotónio, which serves our operation and
serves the village. I love that our back of house is also a service to our
neighbors. That's circular economy in its plainest clothes.
Now, standards. Let me tell you how I think about them.
A standard is a promise we've made to every future guest based on what we've
delivered to past ones. When housekeeping prepares a house, they're not cleaning a
room. They're keeping a promise. The guest paid for the Craveral of the photographs
and the reviews. Every detail that's right, the bed impeccable, the
kitchen spotless, the terrace inviting, the amenities complete, keeps the promise.
Every detail that's wrong breaks it. Just a little.
And broken promises accumulate silently.
A guest rarely complains about the small stuff.
They just quietly downgrade their opinion.
And then one day, they book somewhere else, and we never learn why.
So my rule is simple: Details are not small.
In our world, details are everything, because our whole promise is care.
A farm hotel that preaches love of the land but has a dirty pool filter or a
burnt-out bulb on a walkway is a contradiction the guest feels immediately,
even if they can't articulate it. Coherence between what we say and what we do
is the highest standard we have. And when you see something wrong that isn't
your job, a fallen branch on a walkway, a smudged window, litter near the
pool, there are two kinds of team members.
The one who thinks, "Someone should fix that," and the one who fixes it or reports
it within the hour. Craveral was built by the second kind. Be the second kind.
Next module, the farm table and everything we serve.
The plate where the whole philosophy lands.

t: Sustainability in daily practice: what the mission asks of you before lunch
s: We've talked about regeneration as a vision.
Now let's bring it down to earth, literally, because sustainability at Craveiral
isn't a chapter in a report. It's 100 small physical actions every day
done by you.
This module is the playbook. Start with water. We're in the Alentejo.
Water here is not a utility. It's the limiting factor of
everything. The region lives with drought as a neighbor.
That's why the property recycles water, why the gardens are planned around what
this climate actually gives, why every drop matters operationally.
For you, this means report every leak the hour you see it. A dripping tap is small.
A dripping tap for a month is a scandal. Housekeeping.
Washing routines exist for a reason. Follow the dosing. Full loads, always.
Kitchen. Thawing under running water is forbidden. Plan ahead instead.
None of this is glamorous. All of it is the mission in its workloads.
Energy, same logic. Air conditioning in an empty house is money and carbon
evaporating together. Check, switch off, close.
Lights on walkways and common areas have their schedules.
If you see waste, flag it. The heated indoor pool is one of our biggest energy
commitments. We spend it gladly for guest comfort, which is exactly why we don't
waste a watt elsewhere. Waste, and here I want to change how you
see it. At Craveiral, there's no such thing as throwing away.
There is only routing. Organic scraps route to compost, and compost routes to the
farm, and the farm routes to the kitchen.
You're not discarding a carrot top, you're sending it on a round trip.
Glass, plastic, paper, oil. Each has its stream, and mixing
streams out of laziness breaks the circle we brag about.
And before anything becomes waste at all, ask the better question: why did we
over-order, overproduce, over-portion?
The cheapest waste to manage is the one that never happens. Kitchen team.
You know this better than anyone. Full use of the animal, full use of the
vegetable, preservation and fermentation when the garden overwhelms us.
Peak season abundance becoming a winter jam is the most delicious form of
accounting I know. Purchasing. Every euro we spend is a vote for the world
we want. Local first, seasonal first, real first.
When we buy from the honey producer 20 minutes away, from the Vicentino vineyards,
from the fishermen on this coast, the money stays in the territory and comes back
to us as a stronger, more beautiful region that gets across Europe to visit.
When a supplier decision is yours to influence, ask the belong questions.
Does this strengthen the territory? Does the value circulate here?
The answer isn't always yes. Sometimes there's no local option, and financial
sustainability is a value too. But the question must always be asked.
The farm and the land.
4% built, 96% alive, and the 96%
needs allies.
Stay on the walkways and paths and help guests do the same gently.
If your work touches the land, gardening, maintenance, the farm itself, you already
know. No shortcuts with chemicals. Soil is capital.
We feed it or we lose it. And guests.
Here's the delicate part. We never lecture.
Nobody drove from Lisbon to be scolded about towels.
Our way is to make the sustainable choice the beautiful choice.
The organic amenities smell better.
The seasonal dish is the best thing on the menu.
The walk to the beach is lovelier than the drive.
When guests ask, and they ask more every year, especially our international guests,
answer with pride and specifics. The 4%, the 70% from the farm,
the compost circle, the laundry that serves the village.
Specifics, not slogans. The difference between greenwashing and the real thing is
that the real thing has numbers and mud on its boots. Why am I this insistent?
Because coherence is our old brand.
The moment a guest catches a gap between what we preach and what we do, the
regeneration speech next to an overflowing mixed bin,
we're not a farm hotel anymore. We're a marketing exercise with chickens. I refuse.
And I can only refuse with your hands because I'm not the one holding the hose, the
thermostat, or the purchase order. You are.
Sustainability at Craveiral is the sum of who noticed, who bothered, who did it
properly when nobody was checking. One test, and it's yours to keep.
At the end of any shift, ask, "Did the place end my shift a little better
or a little worse because I was here?" Regeneration is just that question
asked by enough people, answered honestly every single day.
Next module, how we speak, the words we use with guests and with each
other, and why they matter more than you think.

t: How we speak: the Craveiral voice
s: This module is about words. It might seem like a strange training topic,
but you'll use words with guests hundreds of times a day, and the words we choose
are as much a part of Craveiral as the pine trees.
A place that talks about the rhythm of the land in the tone of an airport
announcement is a place at war with itself.
So, the Craveiral voice. The principle first: our voice
is calm, warm, concrete, and unhurried, like the place.
We don't gush, we don't perform enthusiasm, we don't sound like a script.
We sound like a person from this land who is glad you came and knows things worth
knowing. That's it. If you're ever unsure how to say something, say it the way
you'd say it to a friend's parents visiting your home. Respectful, warm, real.
Now, some vocabulary, because small word choices carry the whole philosophy.
We say houses, not units or rooms.
Guests sleep in a house with a kitchen and a terrace. The word should honor that.
We say guests, never clients or customers. We covered why.
We say the farm because it is one. A real working farm, not grounds or
landscaping. We say the farm table, and we talk about dishes by where they came
from, not just what they are. And notice the words the brand lives by.
Belong, stay, the rhythm of the land, root to table, the chain.
Use them naturally when they're true, never as decoration.
The same care applies in reverse. Words we avoid: anything that makes us
sound like a resort chain. Amenity, property features, valued guest.
Corporate language is a wall between two people.
Our whole project is taking walls down. And avoid over-promising words.
Perfect, guaranteed, always. The Alentejo has weather. Farms have seasons.
Kitchens have nights. Promise what we control: care, honesty, effort.
Those we can always deliver. Speaking with international guests, and most of our
guests are international. German, Dutch, French, British, American.
Three notes. First, keep English simple and warm.
You don't need perfect grammar, you need clear goodwill.
A genuine, let me find out for you, beats fluent evasion in any language.
Second, teach a little Portuguese when the moment invites it.
Guests love leaving with obrigado, bom dia, the story of the word Craveiral itself.
A field of carnations. It's a gift that costs nothing.
Third, cultures differ in what warmth looks like.
Some guests want conversation. Others want efficiency and privacy.
Both deserve the same care, calibrated. Reading that difference is a skill.
Watch your most experienced colleagues do it. Writing.
Some of you write to guests, emails, messages, responses to questions.
Same voice on paper. Short sentences.
Warm but never syrupy, always concrete.
Not, we look forward to welcoming you soon, as an empty formula, but,
"The pool is heated in October and the trails are at their best.
You're coming at a lovely time." One true, specific sentence outperforms three
ornamental ones, every time. And how we speak to each other.
Because the internal voice becomes the external one, always.
Teams that speak to each other with respect serve guests with grace.
Teams that bark at each other backstage leak that tension into the dining room
within a week. Guests feel it before they can name it.
So, no shouting culture, not even in the kitchen at full throttle. Direct is good.
Sharp is fine under pressure. Disrespectful is never fine.
Disagree openly, decide, move. I'd rather hear an honest, this
isn't working, in a team meeting than a polite silence that costs us a season.
One more thing. How we talk about Craveiral when we're not at Craveiral.
Each of you is the brand at a dinner table, on your own social media, in the
village café. I'm not going to police that. I wouldn't want to.
I'll only say, the stories you tell about this place are the most credible
marketing we will ever have. Infinitely more than anything we buy.
Tell the true ones, including the funny ones, especially the funny ones.
Words, in the end, are hospitality's smallest unit. A stay is thousands of them.
Choose them the way the kitchen chooses tomatoes.
In season, close to home, and real.
Last module coming up,
and it's the one I care most about getting right.
How we lead, how we work together, and what I expect from you.
And you should expect from me.

t: Leadership, autonomy, and how we work together
s: Last module, and I've saved the most important conversation for the end:
how we work together. Not the org chart, the real thing.
What I believe about leading people, what I expect from you, and what you have
every right to expect from me. Let me start with a confession.
Nobody taught me hospitality management.
I was a lawyer who fell in love with a field of carnations.
Almost everything I know about running this place, I learned by doing it and by
getting it wrong first. So when I talk about mistakes, I'm not being generous from
some throne of perfection. I'm speaking as this company's most experienced maker of
mistakes. Here is my first principle: I'd rather correct your decision than
make all the decisions. You are the person on the ground, in front of the guest,
with the pan on the fire, with the room to prepare.
You see things I will never see from Lisbon or from a spreadsheet.
If you wait for permission for every judgment call, we become slow and worse.
You stop thinking, because why think when someone above you does it for you?
So the rule is when the guest is in front of you and something needs solving, solve
it. Use the values as your compass.
The long game, the relationship, the coherence between what we say and what we do.
If your solution costs a bottle of wine or a free dessert to save a guest's
evening, do it. Tell your manager after.
I will never, ever punish someone for a generous decision made in good faith for a
guest. Never.
Second principle. The mistake is not the problem. Hiding it is.
In eight years of building and eight more of operating, I've seen every kind of
mistake. Doubles booked, dishes burnt, reservations lost, pipes open
at the wrong moment. Here's what I know. A mistake caught early is an anecdote.
A mistake hidden is a crisis. So the deal between us is this.
You bring me the problem while it's small, and I bring you calm, help, and zero
drama. You hide it until it explodes, and then we have two problems, and the second
one is trust. Speak early. Always.
This applies upward too, by the way. When I'm wrong, tell me.
I promise you it won't be career limiting.
The people who've challenged me best are the people I trust most today. Third.
Standards are how we respect each other. I ask a lot. You know this.
The details, the coherence, the promise-keeping.
Module 6 wasn't gentle. But understand why.
High standards are a form of respect.
Respect for the guests who paid us their trust.
Respect for the colleague whose work your work either lifts or undermines.
Because in a place like this, everything touches everything.
A late room delays a check-in, delays dinner, sours an evening.
And respect for yourself. Nobody feels proud going home from sloppy work, and pride
in work is one of the great pleasures of life.
I want Raverello to be the hardest job some of you ever love. Fourth.
We grow people, not just vegetables.
The regeneration we preach for soil applies to careers.
I want people from São Teotónio and Odemira to build real professional lives here
without leaving their land. That's social sustainability with names
and faces. If you want to learn another section, another skill, wine,
English, numbers, say so. The person cleaning houses today can be running
housekeeping in three years. Versions of that sentence have already come true here
more than once. My commitment. We will always prefer to promote from within,
and your ambition is welcome here.
What I ask in return is that you teach others what you learn.
Knowledge that stays in one head is knowledge the team doesn't have.
Fifth, and this one goes both directions. Well-being is non-negotiable.
I said it in the values module, and I'll close with it.
This industry has a long, ugly tradition of burning people out and calling it
fashion. Not here. Not on my watch.
Breaks are real, days off are real, the schedule is human, and if it ever
isn't,
escalate it. To me, if needed.
I would rather run at slightly lower capacity than run on exhausted people, because
exhausted people can't give warmth, and warmth is our entire product.
And between yourselves, watch out for each other.
Cover for the colleague having a hard week. They'll cover you in yours.
The team is the first community we regenerate. Let me land this whole thing.
Sixteen years ago, there was a field of carnations and a lawyer with a dream that
most sensible people found ridiculous.
Today, there are 38 houses full of stories, a farm that feeds hundreds of people a
week, a beach bar on the sand, a table inside a museum in Lisbon, weddings
under our pines, and a team, you, that carries all of it.
None of it was inevitable. All of it came from believing that a place well cared
for cares for those who inhabit it.
