And then working season after season as if that were true.
It turned out it was. You are part of that now. Not employed by it.
Part of it. And my deepest hope for your time here is the same
thing we promise the guests. Because it turns out the brand was never just for
them. Fica. Pertence. Stay. Belong.
Thank you for listening to all of this.
Now,
let's get to work.

t: Why we're here: my story, and the story of Craveiral
s: Hello, I'm Pedro, and if you're watching this, it's because you're part of
Craveral. Maybe you started this week, maybe you've been with us for years.
Either way, I want to start at the beginning.
Because everything we do here, every decision we make, every plate we serve,
every bed we prepare, it all comes from one story.
And I think you deserve to hear it from me. 20 years ago, I was a lawyer in Lisbon.
I still am, actually. I never stopped.
But somewhere along the way, I realized that the life I was building was missing
something. I had the office, I had the career, I had everything that's supposed to
add up to success. And I kept dreaming about land, about farming, about getting my
hands in the soil. It sounds romantic when I say it now.
Believe me, it didn't feel romantic when I was learning how hard farming actually
is. And then, one spring day, I found a field.
A field of carnations near São Teotónio, on the Costa Vicentina.
In Portuguese, a field of carnations is a craveral.
That's where the name comes from. It's not a marketing invention, it's literally
what the land was. I remember standing in that field and thinking, "This is it.
This is the place." Nine hectares of wild Alentejo, minutes from some of the most
beautiful, unspoiled coastline in Europe. No neighbors in sight.
Sky so clear at night that guests still stop me on the walkways to point at the
stars. That was 2010. We opened in 2018. Eight years.
Let that sink in for a moment. Eight years between the dream and the first guest.
Eight years of licensing, of building, of doubting, of running out of money and
finding it again, of convincing architects and engineers and banks and, honestly,
my own family, that a lawyer from Lisbon could build something real in rural
Odemira.
Why am I telling you this? Not for sympathy.
I'm telling you because I need you to understand something fundamental.
Craveral was not built to be a hotel.
It was built to be a relationship with a piece of land.
The hotel is how we sustain that relationship. That order matters.
Land first, hotel second. When you understand that, a hundred small decisions we
make year suddenly make sense. Look at how the place is built.
We have nine hectares. Do you know how much of it is constructed? 4%.
Four.
Everything else is farm, orchard, garden, pine forest, open space.
We could have built more houses. We could have made more money per square meter.
We chose not to, because of the emptiness, the space, the silence at night.
That is the product.
Guests don't come here despite the fact that we built so little.
They come because of it. The houses themselves, 38 of them, are connected by raised
wooden walkways. Have you ever wondered why we built walkways instead of just
paving paths? Because raised wood lets the land breathe underneath.
Water flows, plants grow, the soil stays alive.
Even the way you walk to your house here is a decision about respecting the land.
Here's the phrase I want you to remember from this first module.
We say it in everything belonging to us. We do not own the land.
We belong to it for a while. Think about what that means for your work.
If we own the land, our job would be to extract value from it, get the most out of
it as fast as possible.
But if we belong to it, then our job is to leave it better than we found it.
Better soil, better water, a stronger village, a team that grows.
Guests who leave a little more connected to something real than when they arrived.
That's not a slogan for me. I gave up a quieter, easier life for this idea.
And every person who works at Craveral is, whether you signed up for it or not,
part of that same idea now. One more thing before we move on.
People sometimes ask me, "Pedro, was it worth it?
Eight years, all that risk, all that stress?" And I always answer the same way.
I've watched a child collect eggs in the morning and run to show her parents like
she'd found treasure. I've watched a couple get married under our pine trees.
I've watched people from the village find good, stable work five minutes from home
in a region where that is not a small thing.
So yes, every single day, it's worth it.

t: Our vision, our mission, and the chain
s: Welcome back. In this module, I want to explain Belong.
You've seen the word on our materials, in our communication, maybe on my email
signature, Belong, giving shape to meaning.
And I know that for some of you, it might sound like abstract branding words.
So let me make it very concrete. Belong was born in 2012 as an
idea before Craveral even opened.
It came from a simple conviction, and I want you to hear this sentence properly
because it's the foundation of everything.
"A place well cared for cares for those who inhabit it." Say it to yourself, "A
place well cared for cares for those who inhabit it." It works in both directions.
If we take care of this land, this village, this region, the land, the
village, and the region will take care of us, of our business, of our jobs, of
our families, of our guests. So, what is Belong in practice?
Belong is the signature brand that connects everything we do.
Craveral Farmhouse is the heart of it, but there's also our beach bar down on the
beach, minutes from here. There's the Mesa do Cam, our restaurant at the Gulbenkian
Foundation in Lisbon. There's our catering and events operation, which takes our
table to houses, companies, and celebrations.
And there's the shop and the laundry, which serve not just our guests, but the
village of São Teotónio itself. Different places, different teams, different
customers. One gesture. And the gesture is always the same,
to bring those who eat closer to those who grow. Now, our vision.
Every serious organization has one, and ours is exactly one line, "To regenerate
the territory through a circular economy." Let me unpack those two ideas because
they are not decoration, they're instructions.
Regenerate the territory, not preserve, not don't damage. Regenerate.
That means actively giving back more than we take.
Soil that gets richer each year because we compost.
Water that gets recycled through the property.
Young people who can stay in Odemira because there's meaningful work here.
A food culture that gets stronger because we buy from the shepherd, the fisherman,
the winemaker down the road. When we say regeneration, we mean all of it,
environmental, social, and economic. The land, the people, the money.
All three have to get healthier together. And circular economy.
This means the value we create goes around in a circle instead of leaking out.
The farm feeds the restaurant. The restaurant's organic waste goes back to the
compost, and the compost feeds the farm.
The hotel brings guests, the guests discover the region.
The region's producers sell to our kitchens and our shop.
The laundry serves the hotel and the village.
Money that comes into Craveral doesn't fly off to some headquarters far away.
It circulates here in this territory. That's the circle.
Every time you choose a local supplier, every time you send scraps to compost
instead of the bin, every time you recommend a village restaurant to a guest, you
are turning that wheel. Our mission then is what we do every day to serve
that vision. We provide a space where our community, including our guests, can
connect through agriculture, gastronomy, hospitality, and nature.
Notice the word connect. We're not in the accommodation business.
We're not even in the food business, strictly speaking.
We are in the connection business. A guest sleeps in one of our houses.
Fine, that's a bed. But a guest who picks a tomato in the garden and eats it that
evening at the farm table, that's a connection.
A guest whose child feeds the animals in the morning, connection.
A guest who takes a bottle of local wine home and tells a story of the vineyard at
their dinner table in Berlin or Amsterdam, that's the connection traveling onwards.
There's a phrase we use in Belong that I want to teach you because it should change
how you talk about your own work. We say, "The protagonist is the chain, not
the name." What does that mean? It means that before the plate, there is a
grower. Before the room, there is someone who tended the land.
Before the wine, there's a family that's been making it for generations.
Our job, your job, is to tell that whole chain, the shepherd, the
garden, the vineyard, the community, because that's where the value lives.
When a guest asks about a dish, don't just name it. Tell them where it came from.
"These courgettes were picked this morning about 80 meters from where you're
sitting." I've watched guests' faces change when they hear that.
It transforms a meal into a story they'll retell for years.
And notice what that phrase also says.
Not the name, not Craveral's name, not Belong's name, not my name.
We are not the heroes of this story. The land is. The producers are.
Our guests, when they connect with it, they are. We're the ones who set the table.
So here's my ask from this module. From today, when someone asks what you do,
I'd love you to be able to say more than, "I work at a hotel." You work at a
project that's trying to prove that hospitality can heal a territory instead of
consuming it. Whatever your role, kitchen, housekeeping, reception, farm,
laundry, beach bar, you are part of that proof.
Next module, our values. Not as a poster on a wall, but as decisions you'll make
this week.
